content: Dysmenorrhoea refers to painful menstrual cramps originating from the uterus, which is a prevalent gynecological issue that can significantly impair a person's quality of life. The standard medical treatments for dysmenorrhoea include oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), both of which work by reducing prostaglandin levels. While these therapies are generally effective, they fail to provide relief in approximately 20-25% of cases. For individuals who do not respond to these treatments, surgical options have been explored. Two surgical procedures, uterine nerve ablation (UNA) and presacral neurectomy (PSN), have gained traction in recent years due to advancements in laparoscopic techniques. These surgeries aim to disrupt the majority of sensory nerve fibers in the cervix that transmit pain signals. Observational studies have supported the use of these procedures for primary dysmenorrhoea. However, it is important to note that these surgeries only partially interrupt the sensory nerve fibers in the pelvic region, which means they may not provide complete relief for all individuals with dysmenorrhoea. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of surgical interruption of pelvic nerve pathways in treating both primary and secondary dysmenorrhoea and to identify the most effective surgical approach. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering studies published up to late 2003. Additional efforts were made to identify relevant trials through other sources, and authors of included studies were contacted for further information when necessary. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different surgical techniques for interrupting pelvic nerve pathways, using both open and laparoscopic methods, in the treatment of primary and secondary dysmenorrhoea. The primary outcomes assessed were pain relief and adverse effects. Eleven RCTs were initially identified, but two were excluded due to methodological issues. Of the remaining nine trials, eight were included in a meta-analysis, while the results of one trial were discussed separately due to incompatible data formats. Five trials investigated laparoscopic uterine nerve ablation (LUNA), two examined laparoscopic presacral neurectomy (LPSN), and two focused on open presacral neurectomy (PSN). For primary dysmenorrhoea, there was some evidence suggesting that LUNA was effective when compared to no treatment or a control group. However, when comparing LUNA to LPSN, no significant difference in short-term pain relief was observed. In the long term, LPSN was found to be significantly more effective than LUNA. For secondary dysmenorrhoea, six RCTs focused on cases associated with endometriosis, while one included women with uterine myomas. When LUNA was combined with surgical treatment of endometrial implants, it did not provide additional pain relief compared to surgical treatment of endometriosis alone. In contrast, PSN combined with endometriosis treatment showed an overall improvement in pain relief compared to endometriosis treatment alone, although this benefit appeared to be specific to laparoscopic procedures and limited to midline abdominal pain. Adverse events were more common with PSN, with constipation being the most frequently reported complication. However, this side effect often resolved spontaneously over time. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend the routine use of nerve interruption procedures for managing dysmenorrhoea, regardless of its underlying cause. They emphasized the need for future randomized controlled trials with robust methodologies and adequate sample sizes to better evaluate the efficacy and safety of these surgical interventions.
